section_summary: This section combines wartime intelligence and administrative records on Japanese defenses, military organization, war finance, industrial production, and strategic geography, including Tokyo antiaircraft defenses and annotated maps of Hokkaido, Kobe, and Tokyo. It also contains correspondence about a purported Japanese reorganization plan, military appointments, civilian evacuation, and information volunteered by former residents of Japan. The final twenty-two pages begin an Allied research report analyzing bushido, spiritual training, the offensive spirit, refusal to surrender, revenge, and ceremonial days in Japanese military psychology.

subfiles.title: Eastern Siberian harbours report, concluding page
subfiles.about: Concludes an assessment of harbours and potential naval and seaplane facilities in eastern Siberia.
subfiles.summary: The page describes navigational limitations, mine vulnerability, depth, capacity, garrison strength, and seaplane use at several eastern Siberian anchorages. It emphasizes the strategic proximity of Imperial Harbour to Hokkaido and comments on Konstantin and De-Kastri bays.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Spanish minister's opinion on Japanese affairs
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a Justice Department letter reporting the Spanish minister in Shanghai's views on Japanese affairs.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records file reference 894.20/279 and identifies a Justice Department letter dated April 24, 1942. The original was filed under 894.00/1156.

subfiles.title: Referral note concerning John White's inquiry
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Routes an inquiry for reply because Clement Dunn was ill or absent.
subfiles.summary: The brief internal note states that Dunn was ill and asks another office to answer the communication. Departmental receipt and Far Eastern Affairs stamps date its handling to May 15, 1942.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about a Rational Plan for the Reorganization of Japan
subfiles.about: Requests information about an alleged 1919 Japanese plan asserting a state right to wage expansionist war.
subfiles.summary: White recalls his acquaintance with Dunn from Montevideo and asks the Department to investigate a purported Rational Plan for the Reorganization of Japan. He seeks its origins, authorship, provisions, and the context of its claim that war could be made against states with excessively extensive or inhumanly administered territories.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning the alleged Japanese Reorganization Plan
subfiles.about: Reports that State Department files contain no evidence of the alleged 1919 Japanese reorganization plan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says a search of Department records, including Tokyo embassy despatches for 1919, found no such political plan. He distinguishes the allegation from documented Japanese efforts to rationalize munitions production, mobilize industry, and regiment the economy for war, while allowing that individuals may have privately expressed similar views.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Hornbeck's reply
subfiles.about: Thanks Hornbeck for researching the alleged Japanese Reorganization Plan.
subfiles.summary: White expresses appreciation for the care and promptness of Hornbeck's May 21 response. The letter was sent from Mexico City through the American Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding information on Tokyo antiaircraft batteries
subfiles.about: Forwards W. Garland Richardson's memorandum and map concerning Tokyo antiaircraft batteries and the April 18, 1942 raid.
subfiles.summary: Chase, writing aboard the exchange ship Gripsholm, encloses a memorandum prepared by former vice consul W. Garland Richardson. Copies were designated for naval and military intelligence, and the material was classified strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Mario Planet's observations of the Tokyo raid and defenses
subfiles.about: Records Chilean correspondent Mario Planet's observations of bomb damage and Japanese antiaircraft positions in Tokyo and Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Planet reported seeing burned houses near Shinagawa Station and bomb damage at the Military Academy and Waseda University after the April 18 raid. He identified modern batteries around Tokyo's belt railway and older batteries around the Imperial Palace, while noting apparent gaps at Shiba Park, the Akasaka Detached Palace, and the Imperial Hotel. He also relayed information from the Argentine naval attaché about a fire at Kobe's Tor Hotel.

subfiles.title: Map of central Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides the central Tokyo map used to locate reported bombing damage and antiaircraft batteries.
subfiles.summary: The map depicts central Tokyo wards, railway stations, parks, shrines, government buildings, schools, and diplomatic facilities. Richardson's memorandum refers to its grid coordinates when identifying observed Japanese defenses and raid damage.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs evaluation of Japanese security documents
subfiles.about: Evaluates OSS photostats of Japanese Foreign Ministry security regulations and the National Defense Security Law.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum agrees with the OSS translator's descriptions and identifies the material as part of a May 29, 1941 Japanese Foreign Office circular to the consulate at Mexicali. It concludes that the documents are not of interest to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: OSS transmittal of Japanese security documents
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese documents received through censorship with an expert's comments.
subfiles.summary: Bruce says the Office of Strategic Services obtained Japanese-language documents through the Office of Censorship and had them examined by a Japanese expert. He forwards the expert's comments to the Department of State under a secret classification.

subfiles.title: OSS expert comments on Japanese secrecy regulations
subfiles.from: Office of Strategic Services Japanese-language expert
subfiles.to: Office of Strategic Services and Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese Foreign Ministry security regulations and identifies an available translation of the National Defense Security Law.
subfiles.summary: The expert explains ministerial and archival responsibility for drafting, copying, guarding, circulating, and accounting for secret documents, including special protection for material withheld from foreign nations. The rules applied with modifications to Japanese diplomatic and consular officials abroad. A separate commentary on the National Defense Security Law was not summarized because OSS already held a complete translation.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing a chart of Japanese fortifications
subfiles.about: Offers a chart of Japanese forts found among papers collected during a 1939–1940 trip to India.
subfiles.summary: Johnson says the enclosed item formed part of a paper issued aboard the Tatsuta Maru on August 9, 1939, during a San Francisco–Yokohama voyage. She asks Roosevelt to place it with the appropriate person, and the material was subsequently copied to the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Laura Johnson's fortifications chart
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the chart of Japanese fortifications and forwards it to the War and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Johnson for submitting the material through the White House. It states that the chart is being made available to both military departments for their information.

subfiles.title: Draft reply concerning an alleged Axis Channel-crossing method
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Johnson's offer of information on a purported new method for Axis armies to cross the English Channel.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that Johnson's February 15, 1943 letter was referred by the White House. It forwards the communication to the War Department and asks that department to reply directly.

subfiles.title: Draft reply concerning Sergeant Major Vouza
subfiles.about: Responds to a proposal that Sergeant Major Vouza receive further recognition for resisting Japanese torture.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Bernhardt's letter and newspaper clipping about Vouza's Silver Star and his protection of Marine positions on Guadalcanal. Her recommendation for additional recognition is forwarded to the Navy Department.

subfiles.title: Navy acknowledgment of Laura Johnson's letter and enclosure
subfiles.from: Chief of Naval Operations, Intelligence Branch
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Laura Johnson's letter and fortifications enclosure from the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The Navy confirms receiving the material forwarded by Assistant Liaison Officer David McK. Key. The memorandum is directed to State Department liaison officer Orme Wilson.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Lieutenant General Hikosaburo Hata
subfiles.about: Reports German coverage of Hikosaburo Hata's appointment as Assistant Chief of the Japanese General Staff.
subfiles.summary: A Berlin DNB report describes Hata as a specialist in European and especially Soviet affairs. It notes his military-attaché experience in Russia, Latvia, Sweden, and Romania and his former leadership of the army press and radio division during the China conflict.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese government revenue and military expenditure
subfiles.about: Provides Japanese revenue and expenditure figures for fiscal years 1940–1944.
subfiles.summary: The telegram tabulates tax, bond, and other revenues in millions of yen for four fiscal years. It also lists general and emergency army and navy expenditures, showing rapid growth in wartime borrowing and military spending.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese borrowing in occupied territories
subfiles.about: Reports plans to finance Japan's 1943–1944 budget through borrowing and asset sales in occupied areas.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese finance minister reportedly proposed raising 3.3 billion yen by public borrowing within occupied territories as a step toward a common Greater East Asian financial system. Another 1.6 billion yen was to come from the sale or lease of materials seized during military operations.

subfiles.title: Filing correction for telegram 5342
subfiles.about: Corrects the filing of a duplicate or partial copy of Bern telegram 5342.
subfiles.summary: The note explains that one copy of telegram 5342 was mistakenly assigned file 894.20/288 and should instead be placed under 103.9166/5779. Staff are instructed to locate and remove the second section and deliver it to Mrs. Shipley for proper filing.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Bank of Japan activity
subfiles.about: Reports Bank of Japan profits, note circulation, government deposits, loans, and Treasury holdings for early 1943.
subfiles.summary: The telegram compares the first six months of 1943 with the same period in 1942. It records substantial increases in profits, banknotes in circulation, government deposits, lending, and the bank's Treasury-note portfolio.

subfiles.title: Request to locate a map of Hokkaido
subfiles.about: Asks whether a Hokkaido map can be supplied to S. H. Dawes for further annotation.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs refers to Vancouver despatch 1537 and notes that Dawes had previously supplied useful information. It asks the Office of the Geographer to provide a map that might help him furnish additional intelligence.

subfiles.title: Recommendation for transmitting maps to Dawes
subfiles.about: Recommends sending Hokkaido maps through the consul general at Vancouver for discretionary delivery to Dawes.
subfiles.summary: The Geographer returns the Dawes file after a telephone conversation. It suggests drafting an instruction enclosing the maps and routing it through the Far Eastern and European divisions.

subfiles.title: Vancouver despatch forwarding Dawes's request
subfiles.about: Forwards S. H. Dawes's request for a Hokkaido map on which to expand earlier intelligence notes.
subfiles.summary: Josselyn recalls Dawes's earlier information about Hokkaido and encloses his new letter from Camp A, Englewood. The consulate had told Dawes that the request was referred to Washington because no suitable map was locally available.

subfiles.title: Dawes's request for a Hokkaido map
subfiles.about: Offers to amplify earlier information about Hokkaido if supplied with a sufficiently large map.
subfiles.summary: Dawes requests preferably a Japanese-language map and says Japanese place names would present no difficulty. He highlights Sapporo's airfield and contrasts its distance from Tokyo with the longer route from the nearest port.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting maps for Dawes
subfiles.to: American consular officer in charge, Vancouver
subfiles.about: Sends international and Japanese maps of Hokkaido for delivery to S. H. Dawes.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards four International Map of the World sheets and a two-sheet photostat of a Japanese prefectural map. The Vancouver officer is asked, if no objection exists, to thank Dawes and give him the maps for his annotations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Ikegai conversion to aircraft-engine production
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram reporting that Ikegai had converted its plant to aircraft and marine-engine work.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Bern telegram 6904 and file 894.659/32 as the location of the original report. Its subject is the complete conversion of the Japanese automobile company's plant to aviation motors and marine-engine parts.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Ikegai industrial conversion
subfiles.about: Reports a German press statement that Ikegai had shifted its entire plant to military-engine production.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that the Japanese automobile company Ikegai was now producing aviation motors and parts for marine engines. The information came through the German press.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese missions to European fronts
subfiles.about: References a report on Japanese military and diplomatic missions visiting European battlefronts.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes missions composed of Japanese army, navy, and air officers as well as diplomats. Their purpose was to inspect all sectors of the European fronts and report the military situation to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Office of the Geographer memorandum supplying Hokkaido maps
subfiles.from: Sophia A. Saucerman, Office of the Geographer
subfiles.about: Provides five map products for possible forwarding to S. H. Dawes.
subfiles.summary: The office supplies four sheets of the International Map of the World covering Hokkaido, three of them uncolored, plus a Japanese prefectural map in photostat. It recommends that Dawes receive them if Far Eastern Affairs and the consul general consider it appropriate.

subfiles.title: Disposition memorandum for Dawes's annotated maps
subfiles.about: Suggests that the annotated Hokkaido maps returned from Vancouver are intended for the War Department.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that the Office of the Geographer originally assembled the maps for Dawes to annotate from personal knowledge. The returned maps are attached in a roll and are presumed to be for military use.

subfiles.title: Vancouver despatch returning annotated Hokkaido maps
subfiles.about: Returns Hokkaido maps annotated by S. H. Dawes together with his explanatory notes.
subfiles.summary: Josselyn reports that the maps were sent to Dawes on November 17 and had now been returned with notations keyed to enclosed notes. The four international sheets and two-sheet Japanese photostat were sent back to Washington under separate cover.

subfiles.title: Memorandum forwarding Hokkaido maps to the War Department
subfiles.about: Transmits the Vancouver despatch, notes, and annotated Hokkaido maps to appropriate War Department authorities.
subfiles.summary: Wilson encloses a copy of confidential despatch 1591 and its written enclosures. The physical maps of Hokkaido are attached for transmission within the War Department.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: political review of the Philippines
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a despatch enclosing a political review of the Philippines prepared by repatriates.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference assigns the item number 894.20/305. It indicates that the original report is filed under 101.0090/3366.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Tokyo's permanent antiaircraft defense
subfiles.about: Relays a Tokyo report describing constant civil-defense training and expectations of renewed bombing.
subfiles.summary: The report says Tokyo's antiaircraft defense had been placed on a permanent footing and that people trained daily in schools, offices, and public places. Despite no Anglo-American overflight since April 1942, the strict passive-defense regime suggested that authorities expected further raids.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese urban evacuation plans
subfiles.about: Reports expedited Japanese plans to evacuate major cities and industrial districts.
subfiles.summary: A Tokyo DNB despatch says the cabinet approved measures to remove civilians from large cities and industrial regions. Government offices were being transferred to the provinces, and workers' housing was to be built in parks and open spaces.

subfiles.title: Vancouver despatch concerning Captain H. P. Rugg
subfiles.about: Reports Rugg's offer of information on Kobe and Osaka and forwards a Japanese map and Tokyo postcard.
subfiles.summary: Rugg, formerly associated with Nippon Yusen Kaisha, offered knowledge of Kobe, Osaka's approaches, and related subjects after being introduced by S. H. Dawes. He left a Japanese map of Kobe and a government postcard showing an aerial view of Tokyo for possible United States use.

subfiles.title: War Department return of Kobe map and Tokyo postcard
subfiles.to: War Department liaison officer with the Department of State
subfiles.about: Returns the Japanese map of Kobe and aerial postcard of Tokyo after Military Intelligence review.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Martin returns both items in response to the State Department's January 26 memorandum. The communication identifies him as chief of the Japanese Empire Branch.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of Rugg's map and postcard
subfiles.about: Lends the War Department Rugg's Japanese map of Kobe and aerial postcard of Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Key explains that the Vancouver consulate received the items from former Nippon Yusen Kaisha captain H. P. Rugg. He requests their return to the Department after they have served the War Department's purpose.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese armament-company responsibility law
subfiles.about: References a telegram concerning a new Japanese law imposing production responsibility on armament companies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies telegram 502 as the source and points to file 894.01/40. The subject concerns legal responsibility for armament production.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese Army appointments
subfiles.about: Translates a TASS report announcing four senior Japanese Army appointments.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports Keisuke Fujie's appointment to command the Eastern Army and Sadamu Shimomura's appointment to the Western Army. Hikosaburo Hata was made head of the General Staff Academy and Ichirō Shichida head of the Academy of Military Sciences.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Sakhalin concessions and fisheries protocol
subfiles.about: References a telegram on Japanese petroleum and coal concessions in northern Sakhalin and extension of a fisheries convention.
subfiles.summary: The sheet notes information about transferring Japanese petroleum and coal concessions in northern Sakhalin. It also mentions a protocol prolonging the relevant fisheries convention for five years and points to file 861b.6363/177.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding The Warrior Tradition report
subfiles.about: Provides Grew with a requested copy of a study on Japanese military psychology.
subfiles.summary: Weckerling encloses The Warrior Tradition as a Present Factor in Japanese Military Psychology in response to Grew's November 22 request. He agrees that it is an excellent exposition of how Japanese authorities inculcated military spirit.

subfiles.title: The Warrior Tradition as a Present Factor in Japanese Military Psychology, Part III
subfiles.from: Allied Translator and Interpreter Section, Southwest Pacific Area
subfiles.about: Analyzes the use of bushido, spiritual training, revenge, nonsurrender, offensive doctrine, and ceremonial observance in Japanese military indoctrination.
subfiles.summary: Research Report No. 76, Part III argues that Japanese leaders sought to transform conscript peasants into modern samurai by combining weapons training with a synthetic bushido ideology stressing loyalty, attack, death, and spiritual superiority. Captured diaries, orders, interrogations, and publications illustrate bayonet training, brutality toward prisoners, contempt for Allied materialism, pressure against surrender, and officially cultivated revenge. The report also describes the military use of imperial anniversaries, ritual, ancestor worship, and ceremonial days to reinforce discipline and morale. This section ends during its discussion of Empire Day and Army Day observances.
